chapters.title: About This Book
paragraphs: A Study in Scarlet, published in 1887, is the novel that introduced the world to Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson. It was written by Arthur Conan Doyle, a young Scottish doctor with more imagination than patients, and it first appeared in a Christmas magazine called Beeton's Annual. The magazine paid Doyle twenty-five pounds for all rights to the story. Almost nobody noticed it. No one, least of all its author, suspected that the tall, thin detective with the violin and the chemistry set would become the most famous detective in all of fiction.

The novel is really two books in one. The first half is a London murder mystery, told by Watson, in which Holmes demonstrates his new science of deduction step by step. The second half flashes back across the Atlantic to the American West, to Utah in the days of the Mormon pioneers, to explain the motive behind the crime. Victorian readers loved this bold structure. Modern readers sometimes find the Utah chapters slower going, but they carry the human heart of the story: a tale of love, fanaticism, and a revenge pursued across a whole continent.

What matters most is what begins here. In these pages Holmes and Watson meet for the first time, take rooms together at 221B Baker Street, and found the most famous partnership in literature. Here too is born the method itself: observation, deduction, knowledge. Every detective who came after, from Hercule Poirot to the forensic heroes of modern television, walks a path that Doyle cut open in this book, and every reader who opens it takes the first step of that journey.

chapters.title: The Meeting at the Laboratory
paragraphs: Dr. John Watson came home from the war a broken man. He had served as an army surgeon in Afghanistan, where a Jezail bullet had passed through his shoulder, and then enteric fever had nearly finished what the bullet began. The government sent him back to England with eleven months' pay and no prospects. He was living in a hotel in London, spending his money too fast, when an old friend named Stamford mentioned a curious fellow who was looking for someone to share the rent of some rooms in Baker Street.

Stamford took Watson to the chemical laboratory of St. Bartholomew's Hospital, and there they found the fellow: a tall, thin young man bent over a row of test tubes, so absorbed that he barely looked up. Suddenly he gave a cry of triumph and ran toward them waving a tube in the air. "I've found it! I've found it," he shouted. "I have found a re-agent which is precipitated by haemoglobin, and by nothing else."

It was a test for bloodstains, the first reliable one ever discovered, and Holmes, for that was his name, Sherlock Holmes, was wild with delight. He explained that in a murder trial the question always arose whether a stain was blood or rust or fruit juice, and now science could answer. He shook Watson's hand with sudden warmth, and Stamford introduced them. Before five minutes had passed, Holmes fixed Watson with his sharp grey eyes and said, quite casually, "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive."

Watson stared. He had told no one in England about his service. Holmes only smiled at his amazement. They talked about the rooms in Baker Street, number 221B, and Holmes warned Watson frankly about his habits: he kept chemicals about, he played the violin at odd hours, he could lie silent on the sofa for days when he was thinking. In return Watson confessed he was a quiet man with few friends. They agreed to share the rooms, and that evening Watson moved his books and his old service revolver into Baker Street.

In the days that followed, Watson studied his new companion the way a naturalist studies a strange animal. He made a list of what Holmes knew and did not know. Of literature, philosophy, and astronomy, Holmes knew nothing at all. Of politics he knew little. But his chemistry was profound, his anatomy accurate though unsystematic, and his knowledge of sensational crime was immense. He seemed to have no interest in ordinary knowledge, only in whatever served his strange profession. When Watson asked him what that profession was, Holmes answered simply that he was a consulting detective, the only one in the world, and that the police came to him when they were out of their depth. Watson laughed at the idea. He would not laugh for long.

Watson, who loved to make lists, drew up a table of his companion's limits, and it became one of the most famous pages in detective fiction. Sherlock Holmes's limits, as Watson recorded them: 1. Knowledge of Literature, nil. 2. Knowledge of Philosophy, nil. 3. Knowledge of Astronomy, nil. 4. Knowledge of Politics, feeble. 5. Knowledge of Botany, variable, well up in belladonna, opium, and poisons generally, knows nothing of practical gardening. 6. Knowledge of Geology, practical but limited, tells at a glance different soils from each other. 7. Knowledge of Chemistry, profound. 8. Knowledge of Anatomy, accurate but unsystematic. 9. Knowledge of Sensational Literature, immense, he appears to know every detail of every horror perpetrated in the century. 10. Plays the violin well. 11. Is an expert singlestick player, boxer, and swordsman. 12. Has a good practical knowledge of British law. Watson stared at his own list and wondered what sort of man he had agreed to live with.

chapters.title: The Science of Deduction
paragraphs: One morning over breakfast, Holmes unfolded his philosophy for Watson, and it changed the way Watson saw the world. A man's brain, Holmes said, is like an empty attic, and a wise man fills it only with the tools he needs, neatly arranged and ready to hand. A fool crams in every piece of lumber that comes his way until nothing useful can be found. From a single drop of water, Holmes declared, a logician could infer an Atlantic or a Niagara without having seen or heard of one or the other. All of life was a great chain, and one link revealed the nature of the whole.

"You see, but you do not observe," Holmes told Watson. "The distinction is clear." To prove it, he asked Watson how many steps led up to their rooms. Watson had climbed them a hundred times and had no idea. Seventeen, said Holmes. He had both seen and observed. This was the whole secret of his art: to notice what everyone else walked past, and to reason backward from the smallest trace to the whole story behind it.

Watson began to understand that his companion was a machine for thinking disguised as a man. Holmes spent his idle hours with the violin, drawing wild, melancholy music from it, or he lay for days on the sofa barely moving, recharging his mind. He had written little monographs on subjects no one else had thought to study, such as the differences between the ashes of various tobaccos, a work illustrated with coloured plates. He kept a bottle of cocaine in a corner of the mantelpiece, and when boredom pressed too hard he reached for a seven-per-cent solution. Watson disapproved, but said nothing yet. He was too fascinated by the mind to quarrel with the habits.

Then came the letter that set everything in motion. It was from Tobias Gregson of Scotland Yard, and it told of a dead man found in an empty house in Brixton, with no wound upon him and no clue to who he was or how he died. Lestrade, another detective from the Yard, had also written, begging for help. Holmes read both letters, his eyes shining, and turned to Watson. "What do you say to a run down to Lauriston Gardens?" he asked. Holmes had a favourite image for the mind. He considered that a man's brain originally is like a little empty attic, and you have to stock it with such furniture as you choose. A fool takes in all the lumber of every sort that he comes across, so that the knowledge which might be useful to him gets crowded out. The skilful workman, by contrast, is very careful indeed as to what he takes into his brain-attic, arranging every tool so it can be found in an instant. It was, Watson thought, the perfect picture of Holmes himself: a mind swept clean of everything that did not serve the work, nothing wasted, nothing forgotten.
Watson seized his hat. The first great case of Sherlock Holmes was about to begin.

chapters.title: The Lauriston Gardens Mystery
paragraphs: The house at 3 Lauriston Gardens, off the Brixton Road, stood empty and waiting. It was a bleak, lonely place, and in its bare dining room, lit by a single candle, lay the body of a well-dressed man of about forty. There was no wound on him, no mark of violence, and yet his face was twisted into an expression of horror and hatred, as if his last moments had been filled with something too terrible to name. Scattered on the floor was a little pile of fine red dust, and on the bare yellow wall above the fireplace, written in letters of blood, was a single word: RACHE.

Gregson and Lestrade were already there, full of competing theories. Holmes ignored them both. He moved around the room on his hands and knees with a tape measure and a magnifying lens, examining the dust, the footprints, the dead man's clothes, even his fingernails. He sniffed at the man's lips. He looked long and hard at the word on the wall. When Lestrade suggested the killer must be a woman, because of the small footprints, Holmes shook his head. When Gregson suggested robbery, Holmes pointed out that the man's purse and watch were untouched.

"Rache is the German for revenge," Holmes said quietly, "so don't lose your time looking for Miss Rachel." The word had been written, he explained, to throw the police off the track, to suggest a political secret society. But the killer had made mistakes. From the length of his stride and the size of his boots, Holmes knew he was a tall, strong man with a florid face. From the red dust on his boots, Holmes knew he had been digging, perhaps a labourer. And from the small, delicate footprints beside the large ones, Holmes knew that the tall man had not come alone.

There was one more discovery, and it was the strangest of all. In the dead man's pocket Holmes found a gold wedding ring, a woman's ring. The dead man had not been married, or so it seemed. Why was he carrying it? Holmes said nothing about his conclusions. He only asked the police to place an advertisement in the newspapers: a gold wedding ring found in Brixton Road, to be claimed at 221B Baker Street by its owner. Then he went home, picked up his violin, and waited. Watson, watching him, could not tell whether his friend was a genius or a madman. The details of that room stayed with Watson for the rest of his life. The dead man's fists were clenched and his arms thrown wide, as though he had fought against something invisible in his last moments. His gold watch and his purse lay untouched in his pockets, which ruled out robbery at once. On the floor Holmes found a woman's plain gold wedding ring, old and worn, and in the dead man's pocket a small cardboard box of white tablets. Nobody at the scene understood what any of it meant. Nobody except the thin young man with the magnifying glass, who moved through the room like a hound on a scent, silent, certain, and already far ahead of them all.
He was about to find out.

chapters.title: The Investigation
paragraphs: Holmes had another secret weapon, and Watson saw it in action during those days: a gang of ragged street boys, the Baker Street Irregulars, who could go anywhere and be noticed by no one. While the official police knocked on front doors, these boys slipped through back alleys, listened in public houses, and watched the cab stands. It was one of them who brought word that a certain driver, new to the district and asking strange questions, had been seen near Brixton on the night of the murder. Holmes paid the boy a shilling and smiled like a general whose scouts had found the enemy.", "\"The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes,\" Holmes remarked, as they waited for the ring's owner to appear. It was his favourite complaint against the human race. People looked at a cab in the street and saw only a cab. Holmes looked at the same cab and saw the driver's history written in the wear of his boots and the patches on his coat. The police, he said, saw but did not observe, and so the obvious escaped them.

The obvious, in this case, was the cab. A cab had waited outside the empty house that night; its tracks were clear in the soft earth of the garden. Someone had driven the dead man to Lauriston Gardens and waited. Holmes sent out his unofficial agents, a gang of ragged street boys he called his Baker Street division, to find every cabman who had been near Brixton that night. Within a day they had a name: a driver who had picked up a fare, a tall gentleman in a long coat, and driven him to Lauriston Gardens.

Then the trap was sprung. An old woman came to Baker Street to claim the wedding ring, answering the advertisement. Holmes, who had been expecting a man, was for a moment thrown off. But he followed her when she left, disguised and on foot, and though she gave him the slip by jumping into a cab, he was not discouraged. He had seen enough. That evening, as Watson sat reading, there came a knock, and a rough-looking cabman was shown in. He had come about the ring, he said. Holmes smiled, slipped a pair of handcuffs onto his wrists before he could move, and said, "Mr. Jefferson Hope, I presume."

The cabman did not resist. He looked at Holmes with something like admiration. "If there's a man in England who could have caught me, it's you," he said. "I've been hunted across two continents, and I've done what I set out to do." Watson stared at the prisoner, and then at his friend. In a single week, this strange young chemist had done what all of Scotland Yard could not. But who was the dead man, and what was the revenge written in blood on the wall? For that, they would have to travel back twenty years, to the deserts of Utah.

chapters.title: Jefferson Hope's Story
paragraphs: Jefferson Hope had once been a young hunter and guide in the American West, a free man of the mountains. Twenty years before, crossing the desert with a wagon train, he had found a man and a little girl dying of thirst among the rocks: John Ferrier and his granddaughter Lucy. Hope saved them, and would have led them to safety, but the rescue party that found them was a band of Mormon pioneers, led by their Prophet, Brigham Young. The Mormons took Ferrier and Lucy in, but their charity had a price: they must adopt the Mormon faith and live under Mormon law.

Years passed. Ferrier grew rich, and Lucy grew into a beautiful young woman, and she and Jefferson Hope fell deeply in love. But the Mormon elders had other plans. Lucy was ordered to marry one of the Prophet's chosen sons, Enoch Drebber, a cruel and powerful man. When Ferrier protested, he was found murdered, and Lucy was carried off to a forced marriage. She died within a month, of a broken heart, and was buried in Mormon ground. Jefferson Hope, who had been away hunting when it happened, came back to find everything he loved destroyed.

Hope swore an oath that day that he would follow Drebber and his accomplice, Joseph Stangerson, to the ends of the earth. For years he hunted them across America. They fled from city to city, always one step ahead, until at last they crossed the ocean to London, believing themselves safe. But Hope followed. He took work as a cab driver, learned the streets of London, and waited his chance. When he finally got Drebber alone in his cab, he drove him to the empty house in Lauriston Gardens and confronted him.

There was no knife, no pistol. Hope had prepared something colder. He carried with him a small box containing two pills, identical in appearance. One was a deadly poison; the other was harmless. He offered Drebber the choice, as Drebber had once offered Lucy no choice at all. Drebber chose, swallowed, and died within minutes, his face frozen in that mask of horror the police had found. Stangerson, the second man, was stabbed later in his hotel room when he resisted. The word RACHE on the wall was Hope's signature: revenge, written in the blood of the guilty.

Holmes listened to the whole story in silence. When Hope finished, the detective shook his head. It was a terrible tale, he said, and a just revenge by the law of the desert, but it was still murder by the law of England. Life in Utah under the Prophet was a gilded cage. Ferrier was forbidden to leave, forbidden to speak against the elders, and watched day and night by the dreaded Danites, the Avenging Angels of the church, who punished disobedience with silent murder. When Ferrier's defiance became open, a message was nailed to his door giving him thirty days to surrender Lucy to her forced marriage. Hope, returning from the mountains, found Ferrier shot dead and Lucy already wedded to Drebber. He arrived too late for everything except revenge. He followed Drebber and Stangerson first to Nevada, then to St. Louis, then to Chicago, working as a labourer and a guide, anything that kept him alive, while his hatred never cooled for a single day. When the two men sailed for Europe, Hope worked his passage as a ship's hand. There was no corner of the earth, he told Holmes, where they could hide from him.
Hope only smiled. He had lived for this revenge for twenty years, he said, and now that it was done, he did not care what became of him.

chapters.title: The Two Pills
paragraphs: That night, in the sitting room at Baker Street, Holmes laid the little box with the two pills on the table and explained everything to Watson. The poison, he said, was a powerful alkaloid, tasteless and quick. Hope had meant Drebber to choose his own fate, and Drebber had chosen death. It was, Holmes admitted, one of the strangest cases he had ever handled, and the cleverest revenge he had ever seen.

But Jefferson Hope would never stand trial. The years of hardship, the exposure, the burning hatred he had carried for two decades had ruined his heart. In his cell, before the trial could begin, he was found dead of a diseased heart, an aneurysm that burst in the night. He died, as he had lived since Lucy's death, alone and unjudged by any court but his own conscience.

Gregson and Lestrade, of course, took all the credit in the newspapers. Their names were praised, their cleverness celebrated, while the name of Sherlock Holmes appeared nowhere. Watson was furious at the injustice, but Holmes only laughed. He cared nothing for fame, he said. He had solved the problem, and that was reward enough. What did it matter who got the applause?

As Watson wrote down the story of those strange weeks, he thought about what he had witnessed. A murder without a wound, a word written in blood, a revenge twenty years in the making, all unravelled by a young man with a magnifying glass and a mind like a steel trap. And he remembered Holmes's words on that first night in Baker Street, words that would echo through all the adventures to come: there is a scarlet thread of murder running through the colourless skein of life, and it is the detective's duty to unravel it, and isolate it, and expose every inch of it. Before the end, Holmes had one more lesson for his friend. The police, he said, would take the credit, and the newspapers would praise Gregson and Lestrade, and none of it mattered in the least. What mattered was the chain of reasoning, unbroken from the first footprint in the garden to the last pill in the box. A case, Holmes said, is like a skein of tangled thread, and the detective's whole work is to find the one loose end and follow it patiently to the truth. Watson, listening, understood at last what he had been privileged to witness: not merely the capture of a murderer, but the first public demonstration of a new science.
Watson laid down his pen. He had studied, as Holmes would say, in scarlet.

chapters.title: The King of Bohemia
paragraphs: After the affair at Lauriston Gardens and its strange sequel in the American West, Dr. Watson married and left Baker Street for a medical practice of his own in the Paddington district. Holmes stayed behind in their old rooms, buried in his chemical researches and his violin, and for a time the two friends saw little of one another. Then, one March evening, Watson called at 221B to find his old companion entertaining a visitor who had come masked, and who would not give his name. The man was tall and imposing, with the unmistakable bearing of a prince and a strong German accent, and he carried himself as one accustomed to being obeyed. Holmes listened to his halting, embarrassed story, and when the mask was at last removed, the visitor stood revealed as a king: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein and hereditary King of Bohemia.

The King's trouble was an old photograph. Five years before, during a stay in Warsaw, he had known a young woman of great beauty and talent, and in an hour of folly he had allowed himself to be photographed with her, side by side, in a single cabinet picture. The woman was Irene Adler, whom the King described, with a dark look, as a well-known adventuress, and the photograph was in her hands. She had written to him that on the day his marriage was publicly announced she would send the picture to the family of his intended bride. The marriage was of the greatest consequence: he was engaged to Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, second daughter of the King of Scandinavia, a match that required an unsullied name, and the photograph would shatter it. The King begged Holmes, for the sake of his house and his honour, to recover it by any means.

Holmes listened without a flicker of surprise. A photograph, he observed, was a small thing, and a woman's anger could be a very large one. The King had already tried the obvious roads: he had offered money, and she had refused it; he had tried theft, sending agents to search her house, and she had been too clever for them; he had even tried to have her waylaid on the road, and that too had failed. Every attempt had left the photograph exactly where it was, in Irene Adler's possession, and had only taught her how precious it was. Holmes took the case, and before the King left he had gathered what the man knew of his adversary: an American by birth, born in New Jersey in the year 1858, a contralto of some renown who had sung at La Scala in Milan and at the Imperial Opera in Warsaw, retired now from the stage and living quietly in London at Briony Lodge, Serpentine Avenue, in St. John's Wood.

The next morning Holmes began his work in his own fashion. He came down to breakfast transformed: unshaven, red-faced, and smelling of beer, dressed as a drunken, out-of-work groom, and Watson barely knew him. For the whole day he loitered about the stables and mews near Briony Lodge, gossiping with the ostlers, and by evening he had a complete picture of the lady's habits. She was, everyone agreed, a beautiful woman, and her singing, though heard only in private now, was said to be extraordinary. One gentleman visited her daily, a lawyer named Godfrey Norton, of the Inner Temple, and the talk of the mews was that an engagement was in the air. She drove out or walked every day and returned at seven for dinner. That was all Holmes needed. He had found the keyhole; now he needed the key.

The next morning brought the adventure Holmes had half expected and wholly welcomed. He followed Irene Adler's carriage through London at a furious pace to St. Monica's Church in the Edgware Road, and there he witnessed a small, hurried wedding: Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton were married before a handful of witnesses. The clergyman was in some confusion, the clerk having failed to appear, and Holmes, quick as ever, was pressed into service as a witness, signing his name and handing a sovereign to the bride's attendant before slipping away. He returned to Baker Street in high spirits. The marriage changed nothing, he told Watson, except to add one more motive: a married woman with a husband's interests at heart might part with the photograph more readily than a single one.

That afternoon Holmes laid the plan before Watson, and Watson's part in it was simple but essential. At seven that evening, when Irene Adler would be at dinner, they would be waiting outside Briony Lodge. Holmes would go in disguise as a simple clergyman, fallen among rough companions, and at a signal Watson was to throw a plumber's smoke-rocket through the drawing-room window and raise the cry of fire. The street would fill in a minute, and in the panic of a fire a woman's first instinct, Holmes explained, is to save what she loves most. When she rushed to the photograph's hiding place, he would see where it was. All Watson had to do was to be in Baker Street by three o'clock, and then to follow Holmes's lead without a question.

Watson never forgot the strangeness of that visitor. The man had come in a closed brougham, his face hidden behind a half-mask, and he had climbed the seventeen steps to the sitting room with the heavy tread of one carrying a burden heavier than his body. His voice was deep and harsh, with the clipped consonants of a German who has learned English late, and his manner was that of a man used to command, now forced to beg. Holmes received him with the calm of a physician, offered him a chair, and waited. The mask, Holmes remarked dryly, was a poor disguise for a man who wished to be unknown, for it drew the eye to everything it tried to hide. The visitor tore it off with an impatient gesture, and there was the King of Bohemia, red-faced and miserable, a great prince brought low by a photograph.

Holmes questioned him as a lawyer questions a witness. Had he tried to buy the photograph back? Yes, and she had laughed at the sum. Had he tried to steal it? Twice his agents had searched Briony Lodge in her absence, and twice they had found nothing. Had he tried the law? She had committed no crime that any court could touch. Had he tried threats? She had answered them with a letter that made his blood run cold. The woman, the King admitted, had but one condition: that he leave her alone, and marry whom he pleased, and trouble her no more. She did not want his money. She wanted, he believed, her revenge for being cast aside, and she would take it on the day of his wedding, when the scandal would wound him most. Holmes listened, and Watson saw the slow smile gather on his friend's face.

It was, Holmes said afterward, a case with features of the very highest interest. Here was a king, a man who commanded armies and moved in the orbit of emperors, held helpless by a single woman with a single picture. The photograph had been taken in Warsaw five years before, in the days when the King, then a young prince travelling incognito, had fallen under the spell of the beautiful contralto. It showed the two of them side by side, unmistakable, intimate, and in the wrong hands it would end the Bohemian marriage before it began. The King was vain, impulsive, and terrified of scandal, and Irene Adler, whom he had tried to treat as a plaything, had proved to be the one person in Europe he could not buy, frighten, or outwit.

When the King had gone, Holmes sat for a long time in his armchair, his fingertips together, and Watson knew the signs of a mind at work. The case, Holmes said at last, was a duel, and it must be fought with duelling weapons. Force had failed; cunning had failed; what remained was to find the photograph's hiding place, and to take it before the lady knew it was in danger. The best information about a woman, he observed, is to be had not from her friends but from the servants' gossip of the neighbourhood, and the best disguise for gathering it is the livery of a groom. Watson laughed, but Holmes was already opening his box of disguises, and by the next morning the great detective had vanished into the stables of St. John's Wood.

The next morning Watson watched the transformation with delight. Holmes's box of disguises stood open on the bed, and in an hour the fastidious detective had become a red-faced, shambling groom, complete with a slouch, a leer, and a smell of the stable-yard that made Watson step back. Holmes explained his philosophy of disguise as he dressed: it is not the clothes that deceive, but the small habits, the way a man holds his hands and takes his drink, and a groom who talks horses is a groom, whatever his Latin. He would spend the day among the ostlers of St. John's Wood, he said, and he would learn everything there was to learn about the lady of Briony Lodge. Watson was to hold himself ready, and to ask no questions until the evening. The game, Holmes said with a grin, had begun, and for once the quarry was not a criminal but a woman.

Before he left that night, the King asked Holmes the question that had been burning in him since Warsaw: what manner of woman was she, that no money and no threat could move her? Holmes answered that she was the rarest thing he had ever been asked to hunt: a person of honour acting in her own defence, and that the King would do well to thank his stars she had chosen revenge in the form of a letter rather than a scandal. The King went away thoughtful, and Watson suspected that, for the first time, the great prince had begun to understand the woman he had wronged.

chapters.title: The Woman
paragraphs: At seven o'clock that evening, in the gathering dusk of Serpentine Avenue, the plan was carried out to the letter. Holmes, disguised as a kindly clergyman with a blackened eye, loitered near Briony Lodge and was taken in by Irene Adler's own servants when a staged brawl broke out at her door. The smoke-rocket hissed through the window; Watson raised the cry of fire; the street filled with shouting neighbours, and in the midst of the confusion Irene Adler ran to the wall above the right-hand bell-pull, where a sliding panel concealed a shallow recess. Holmes saw the panel move, saw her hand go to it, and had to restrain himself from seizing the photograph then and there, with too many eyes upon him. He left the house with the crowd, the secret of the hiding place safe in his mind, and told Watson that on the morrow, while the lady was out driving, they would walk in and take it.

Holmes was too confident, and he knew it the instant the night betrayed him. As they parted, a slim young man in the crowd wished them both good night, and Holmes, who never forgot a face, felt a cold touch of doubt. He followed the figure a little way, and the doubt grew into certainty. The next morning, when he and Watson went to Briony Lodge to claim the photograph, the house was empty. Irene Adler and her husband had left London for the Continent the night before. On the mantelpiece of the sitting room, addressed to Mr. Sherlock Holmes, lay a letter, and beside it a photograph of Irene Adler alone. Holmes read the letter aloud to Watson, and the reading of it was the most extraordinary moment of his career.

The letter was a masterpiece of cool triumph. Irene Adler wrote that she had recognized Holmes long before the fire was ever lit: the drunken groom who had opened her carriage door that morning, the clergyman who had received a black eye at her threshold, were one and the same man, and she had seen through both disguises. She had been warned that he would come, and when the cry of fire rose she had let him see the hiding place on purpose, knowing that she would be gone before morning. She had followed him home that night, she wrote, for she was the slim youth who had bidden him good night in the street, and she knew where he lived. She kept the photograph of herself for him, she said, as a souvenir of the one man who had ever come close to outwitting her. And she signed herself, no longer the adventuress of the King's description, but a wife: Irene Norton, born Irene Adler.

Holmes took his defeat with a grace that Watson had never seen in him. When the King of Bohemia came that evening, full of anxiety, Holmes told him plainly that the photograph was gone beyond recovery, and that the lady would never use it against him now. The King, in his relief, pressed Holmes to name his reward, and Holmes named it: he asked for nothing but the photograph of Irene Adler, which the King held in his hand. He carried it home to Baker Street, and there it stayed. He never saw Irene Adler again, and he never tried to. She had beaten him fairly, and he bore her no grudge for it.

It was after this case that Watson noticed the change in his friend. Holmes, who had always spoken of women with a kind of amused contempt, as creatures whose emotions clouded their reason, never laughed about them again. The best plans of Mr. Sherlock Holmes had been beaten by a woman's wit, and he knew it. And from that day on, whenever he spoke of Irene Adler, or whenever he referred to her photograph upon his desk, it was always by the honourable title of the woman. To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman. He had seldom heard him mention her under any other name, and Watson understood at last that in all the world there was exactly one person whom Sherlock Holmes held to be his equal.

Watson thought about the case often in later years, and it seemed to him the most instructive of all their adventures. Irene Adler had done what no criminal, no king, and no Scotland Yard detective had ever done: she had seen Sherlock Holmes whole, disguise and all, and she had outplayed him at his own game, not with cunning but with candour. She had not fled in fear; she had written to him, freely, as one equal to another, and had left him her photograph of her own will. Holmes kept it on his desk for the rest of his life, and Watson believed it reminded him of the one great truth he had learned at Briony Lodge: that a brilliant mind is no match for a brave heart, and that even the most perfect reasoning can be undone by simple human courage.

The days before the attempt were spent in preparation, and Watson watched his friend with a mixture of admiration and unease. Holmes manufactured his smoke-rockets himself, choosing the kind that gives a dense white smoke without flame, and he rehearsed the plan with the care of a stage manager. Watson was to stand in the crowd, throw the rocket through the open window, and shout fire at the top of his voice. It was a deception, Watson objected, a trick played upon a woman. Holmes answered that when one deals with an adversary of the first order, one must meet audacity with audacity, and that the law would never recover what only ingenuity could find. The photograph, he said, was in that house, and before the week was out it would be in his hands.

The night of the fire went as planned, and the morning after brought the reckoning. Holmes woke Watson early with the news that their triumph might be hollow: the slim young man who had bidden them good night had been no bystander, and Holmes, turning the encounter over in the small hours, had grown certain that he had been followed. They hurried to Briony Lodge and found the house dark and silent. The maid who answered the door told them that Mrs. Norton, as she must now be called, had left London the night before with her husband, for the Continent, and would not return. In the sitting room the sliding panel above the bell-pull stood open and empty. The photograph was gone, and with it the woman who had kept it.

The letter explained everything, and Holmes read it twice before he spoke. Irene Adler, now Irene Norton, wrote that she had been warned that the King would employ an agent, and that she had recognized Holmes from the first: the drunken groom who had opened her carriage door, the injured clergyman at her threshold, were one man, and she had seen through him. She had let him believe he had found the hiding place, she said, because she had already decided to leave England, and the photograph was no longer a weapon she had any wish to use. She enclosed her own photograph for him, as a keepsake of the only man who had ever made her take such precautions. She asked only to be left in peace with the husband she loved, and she promised that the King would never hear from her again.

That evening the King of Bohemia came to Baker Street in a state of wild anxiety, and left it in a state of wild relief. He pressed upon Holmes a costly jewel from his own finger, and Holmes refused it with a courtesy that surprised Watson, asking instead for a single thing: the photograph of Irene Adler that lay upon the table. The King gave it gladly, thinking it a small price, and Holmes carried it home like a trophy. Watson kept the picture of that moment for the rest of his life: his friend standing by the fire with the photograph in his hand, beaten fairly and bearing no malice, paying his defeated adversary the highest compliment in his power. He asked for nothing but her picture, and he kept it always.

The photograph stayed on Holmes's desk for the rest of his life, and Watson came to understand what it meant to him. It was not a trophy of a case, for the case had been lost, and it was not a sentimental keepsake, for Holmes had no sentiment in him as other men understand it. It was a reminder, kept where he would see it every day, that the most perfect reasoning in the world can be undone by a brave and honest heart. Irene Adler had not cheated him; she had beaten him fairly, with open eyes and a clear head, and she had left him her picture freely, as one good player leaves a token to another. Of all the thousands who had crossed his path, she alone had earned the title he gave her. She was not a client, not a criminal, not a case. To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman, and Watson, who had seen kings beg and murderers hang, never saw his friend pay any other human being so high an honour.

chapters.title: A Trembling Client
paragraphs: Two years after the Adler affair, Holmes and Watson were woken at dawn by a visitor who had come in a dog-cart and could not wait for the hour. She was a young lady, pale and trembling, dressed in a hurry, with the look of one who has not slept. Holmes needed only a glance at the splashes of mud upon her sleeve to know how she had travelled, and she needed only his first kind words to tell him why. She was Helen Stoner, stepdaughter of Dr. Grimesby Roylott of Stoke Moran, in Surrey, and she said the thing at once, without shame: she was frightened. It was about her sister, she said, and about the speckled band.

Her sister Julia had died two years before, a fortnight before her wedding day, in the bedroom that Helen now occupied. On the night she died, Helen had heard her sister whistle softly in the dark, and then a terrible cry, and then a sound like metal clanging. She had run to the room and found Julia standing in the doorway, her face white with terror, pointing into the air and gasping out words that Helen would never forget: something about a band, a speckled band. Julia died before morning, and no one ever found a wound upon her, or a trace of poison, or any mark of violence at all. The coroner could give no cause. Now Helen herself was to be married, and she had been moved into her sister's old room, and the night before she had heard, at three in the morning, the same low whistle she had heard the night Julia died.

The master of Stoke Moran was Dr. Grimesby Roylott, the last of a violent old family, a man who had practised medicine in Calcutta and returned to England a ruined and embittered widower, married to the girls' mother. When their mother died in a railway accident eight years before, her money had passed to Roylott for his lifetime, so long as the girls lived under his roof, but a yearly sum would come to each daughter on her marriage. Helen was now engaged, and had asked for repairs to the house; Roylott had moved her into Julia's bedroom while the work was done. The doctor kept strange company: a cheetah and a baboon roamed the grounds, and a gang of Indian servants came and went. He was a man of enormous strength and fearful temper who had once thrown a village blacksmith over a parapet into a stream, and the whole countryside went in terror of him.

Holmes had barely begun his questions when the door burst open and the doctor himself stood in the room, huge and glaring, his face mottled with rage. He had followed his stepdaughter to London, and he threatened Holmes with terrible consequences if he meddled in the affairs of Stoke Moran. To show what he could do, he seized the steel poker from the fireplace and bent it in his great hands like a bow. Holmes said nothing until the man had gone. Then he picked up the poker, and with a quiet smile straightened it out again, and told Watson that they would go down to Stoke Moran that very day. The case had become, he said, a matter of life and death, and Helen Stoner's life depended on what they found there.

The inspection of the house told Holmes everything he needed. Julia's bedroom, which Helen now occupied, was a small room with a bed clamped firmly to the floor, so that it could not be moved. Beside the bed hung a bell-pull, but the rope was a dummy: it hung beside a small ventilator that opened not to the outside air, but into the next bedroom, Dr. Roylott's own room. The ventilator was new, far too small to move any air, and the bell-rope had never been connected to any wire. In Roylott's room Holmes found an iron safe, and upon it a small saucer of milk, and beside it a dog's lash with a loop at the end, worn as if something had been tied with it. On the lawn the cheetah and the baboon watched them with yellow eyes. Holmes said very little, but Watson saw that his face had grown grave and set.

That evening, back in London, Holmes laid the whole dreadful picture before Watson. No one could have entered Julia's room from outside: the door was locked from within, the windows were shuttered, and the chimney was barred. Therefore the thing that had killed her had come from inside the house, and there was only one passage by which it could have come: the ventilator that joined her room to the doctor's. The bell-rope hung beside it like a bridge, and the bed was clamped beneath it, so that whatever crossed the bridge would fall exactly upon the sleeper. The saucer of milk and the looped lash told the rest. Holmes would say no more that night, except to ask Watson to bring his service revolver. They would spend the night in Julia's room, in the dark, and they would watch.

Helen Stoner told her story in fragments, and Holmes drew it out of her with a gentleness Watson had rarely seen in him. She was now engaged to be married, she said, and it was this that had set the old terrors moving again. Her stepfather had agreed, grumbling, to have the house repaired, and while the workmen were in her own room she had been moved into the bedroom where her sister had died. She had not wanted to go. She remembered that room too well: the bed clamped to the floor, the strange little ventilator high on the wall, the bell-pull that rang no bell. And two nights before, lying awake in the dark, she had heard it again, the sound she had heard on the night Julia died: a low whistle, soft and clear, at three in the morning.

Holmes's questions were sharp and few. Had Julia spoken of hearing the whistle before she died? Yes, she had mentioned a whistle in the night, and had laughed it off as the wind. Had anyone else heard the metallic clang? Only Helen, who had been awake with a sick headache. What had the doctors said? The village doctor had found no wound, no trace of poison, no mark of any kind, and the coroner had been forced to return a verdict that satisfied no one: death from some unknown nervous shock. Holmes nodded slowly. A death with no wound, he said, is a death that has been arranged, and the arrangement is always the thing to find. He asked about the money, and Helen's answer confirmed his darkest guess: on her marriage, a sum would pass out of her stepfather's hands, and Roylott had been heard to say that no daughter of his should take his money to a husband.

The journey to Stoke Moran was made that same afternoon, and the house matched its master's reputation. It stood in its own grounds, half-hidden by trees, a grey and mouldering pile with the air of a place where time had stopped. On the lawn a cheetah and a great baboon roamed at liberty, and the villagers at Leatherhead crossed themselves when the travellers asked the way. Holmes walked the grounds in silence, noting the windows of the two bedrooms and the ventilator between them, and he spoke barely a word until they stood inside Julia's room. There he examined the clamped bed, the dummy bell-pull, and the little ventilator with the intensity of a jeweller studying a stone, and Watson knew that the case was already solved in his mind.

On the train home Holmes laid the reasoning before Watson, and it was like watching a lock turn. The room was locked from within, the windows shuttered, the chimney barred: therefore no one had entered from outside. The bed could not be moved, and it stood beneath the ventilator and the bell-pull: therefore whatever came through the ventilator would fall upon the sleeper. The ventilator was new, too small to ventilate, and it opened into the doctor's room: therefore it had been made for another purpose. The saucer of milk, the looped lash, the whistle, the clang: each had its place, and together they spelled a single dreadful word. They would spend the night in that room, Holmes said, in the dark, and they would wait for the whistle. And Watson understood that they were going to meet a murderer at his work.

What struck Watson most, looking back, was not the horror of the ventilator or the cunning of the bell-rope, but the gentleness with which Holmes treated the frightened girl who had brought them the case. He who was so cold with kings and so merciless with criminals spoke to Helen Stoner as a brother might speak, and when Roylott burst into the room with his threats and his bent poker, it was for her sake, as much as for justice, that Holmes's face went hard as iron. He knew, even then, that the law could never touch such a murderer: a snake leaves no wound that a coroner can swear to, and a ventilator is only a ventilator until someone proves what passed through it. So he set the law aside, as he had done more than once before, and undertook to meet the murderer at his work, in the dark, with a cane. It was dangerous, it was irregular, and Watson would not have had him do otherwise.

chapters.title: The Speckled Band
paragraphs: They reached Stoke Moran after dark and were shown into Julia's room by Helen Stoner, who then retired to her own chamber with strict orders to bolt the door. Holmes and Watson sat in the darkness without a lamp, in perfect silence, and the hours crawled by. Holmes had brought his cane, and he had placed it across his knees. Watson, with his revolver in his pocket, listened to the ticking of the hours and the night sounds of the old house, and thought of the girl sleeping alone in the next room and of the sister who had died in this same bed. At about three o'clock in the morning, a faint sound broke the stillness: a low, clear whistle, like the one Helen had described. A moment later came the metallic clang that she had heard on the night of her sister's death. Holmes sprang to his feet, lit the candle, and struck furiously at the bell-pull with his cane.

Watson saw it then, and never forgot the sight. Coiled about the bell-pull, its head swaying, was a snake, yellow with brown speckles, the most venomous reptile he had ever seen. Holmes lashed at it again and again, driving it back toward the ventilator, and the creature, maddened by the blows and the light, slipped through the opening into the doctor's room. An instant later a terrible scream rang out from beyond the wall, a cry of mortal agony, and then silence. They burst into Roylott's room to find him seated in his chair, his chin upon his chest, his eyes fixed and staring. Around his head was coiled the speckled band, the swamp adder, its fangs sunk in his forehead. The doctor was dead, killed by the very weapon he had trained for murder.

In the grey light of morning, Holmes explained it all. The swamp adder was the deadliest snake in India, and Roylott, who had learned its handling in Calcutta, had trained it as other men train dogs. The ventilator was its passage, the dummy bell-rope its bridge, and the bed was clamped to the floor so that the sleeper could not move away from the spot where the snake would descend. Each night Roylott put the snake through the ventilator; each morning he called it back with the low whistle, and the saucer of milk lured it into the safe, whose door made the metallic clang. Julia had been killed on the eve of her wedding because her marriage would have taken a yearly sum out of Roylott's hands; Helen, newly engaged, was to be the next. The snake struck the doctor in the dark because Holmes's blows and the sudden light had driven it back through the ventilator in a fury, and it turned upon the first warm hand it found.

They carried the adder back to the safe and closed the iron door upon it. At the inquest the coroner could make little of the death, and Holmes, for his part, told the court only so much as the evidence required. Roylott could never have been proved a murderer in any case, and Holmes felt no great sorrow for the manner of his end. The violence that the man had practised all his life, upon his servants, upon his neighbours, and at last upon his own stepdaughters, had turned in the end upon himself. He had set a trap of living venom, and he had died in it.

Watson wrote the story down as he had written all the others, but this one stayed with him longer than most. He thought of Helen Stoner, who had come to them trembling at dawn and who owed her life to a night of watching in the dark. He thought of the cheetah and the baboon roaming the grounds of Stoke Moran, and of the saucer of milk upon the iron safe, small domestic details that had hidden a design of cold and patient murder. And he thought of Holmes, sitting hour after hour in the black bedroom with a cane across his knees, waiting for a whistle in the night. It seemed to Watson that the whole case was a parable of the evil that Roylott had carried home from India: a speckled band of venom, loosed in the dark against the innocent, and returning at last to the hand that had loosed it.

The waiting was the hardest part, and Watson never forgot those hours. They sat from eleven o'clock in perfect darkness, without a lamp, without a whisper, Holmes motionless with his cane across his knees, Watson with his revolver cold in his pocket. The house settled into silence. Somewhere a clock struck twelve, then one, then two, and each hour seemed to last a night. Holmes sat like a statue, but Watson knew from long experience that his friend was awake and listening with every nerve. Twice a board creaked in the corridor, and twice Watson's heart leapt. Then, at a few minutes past three, the silence broke: a low, clear whistle, soft as a sigh, and a moment later the sharp metallic clang of a heavy door.

The days that followed were strange and quiet. Helen Stoner, freed from the shadow that had hung over her since her sister's death, wept when Holmes told her that she was safe, and Watson thought he had never seen his friend so gentle as he was with that frightened girl. The snake was carried back to the iron safe and the door shut upon it. At the inquest the coroner stared at the dead doctor and the empty rooms and could make nothing of it, and Holmes told the court only what the evidence compelled him to tell. No jury could have convicted a dead man of murder by snake, and no law had a name for what Roylott had done. The village breathed easier, the cheetah and the baboon were sent away, and Stoke Moran stood empty.

Holmes explained the training of the snake to Watson on the way home, and it was the darkest part of the whole dark business. The swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India, had been Roylott's companion since Calcutta, and he had schooled it as other men school dogs. The whistle called it back through the ventilator when its work was done; the saucer of milk rewarded it and lured it into the safe; the looped lash was for handling it without being bitten. On the night they watched, Holmes's blows and the sudden light had driven the maddened creature back through the opening in a fury, and it had struck the first living thing it found in the dark: the hand of the master who had loosed it. Roylott had been killed, Holmes said quietly, by his own weapon, turned against him.

Watson closed the narrative as he had closed the others, but this one left a mark upon him that time never quite effaced. He thought of Julia Stoner, dying in that clamped bed with no wound upon her, and of Helen, who had come to them trembling at dawn and who would now live to marry. He thought of the doctor himself, a man of great gifts gone wholly to ruin, who had carried the violence of his nature from the jungles of India to the quiet lanes of Surrey, and who had died at last by the venom he had nursed. And he thought of Holmes, who had sat through the black hours with a cane across his knees, waiting to meet a murderer in the dark. It seemed to Watson a fitting end to the story of the speckled band: that evil, loosed against the innocent, should return at last to the hand that loosed it, and that justice, denied by every court, should be done by the very instrument of the crime.

On the drive back to London, Holmes was silent for a long time, and Watson did not disturb him. At last his friend spoke, and what he said stayed with Watson for years. Violence, Holmes said, is a debt that is always repaid, and Roylott had been paying his in instalments all his life: the ruined fortune, the fear of the countryside, the cheetah on the lawn, and at last the snake in the ventilator. He had trained a living weapon to do his murder for him, and the weapon had turned in his hand. Helen Stoner married her young man that autumn, and Watson heard that she lived happily, though she never spoke of Stoke Moran. And whenever Watson thought of the case in later years, he thought not of the horror of it, but of the strange and terrible justice of its ending: that the speckled band, loosed in the dark against the innocent, should have returned at last to coil about the head of the man who loosed it.

Watson published the two stories years apart, and he always thought of them as a pair, the two cases that showed the two faces of his friend. In the one, the greatest mind in England was beaten by a woman's wit, and bore his defeat like a gentleman, keeping her photograph as the dearest of his possessions. In the other, that same mind sat through the black hours of a country bedroom and met a murderer in the dark, saving a frightened girl from a death no coroner could have named. Irene Adler and the speckled band: a photograph and a snake, a woman's courage and a villain's venom. Between them they contained everything Watson had learned in his years at Baker Street: that reason is a splendid weapon, but that it is the heart behind it, brave or cruel, that decides whether it saves a life or takes one. And so the chronicles of Sherlock Holmes, which had begun in scarlet with a dead man in an empty house, went on in stranger colours still, and Watson laid down his pen at last with the happy certainty that there were more stories to tell.
